Two results here. The first closes the loop-rescue idea properly. Gold appears before loop onset in only 16% of Let cut-offs, and it's the last equation result in only 1.4%, so a well-timed stop wouldn't rescue these answers. The example shows why: the model derives a negative quantity, can't resolve it, and cycles.

The second result is new. Let answers whose first line defines something close to the question are right far more often: 30.7% in the top overlap tercile against 18.5% in the bottom, with accuracy given finishing at 40.8 against 26.7. That could be easy problems showing up as high overlap, so I won't trust it yet.

The E4 flip gives me a much better tool: Let and Here answers to the same problems, produced by an intervention, so difficulty is held fixed. I'll use it to find what carries the 20-point loss, comparing false equations, dropped needed numbers, step counts and how much of the problem text gets restated. The E1 flip serves as a control, since it changed the register without changing accuracy: a real carrier should move on E4's flipped problems and not on E1's.

I'll also stratify the overlap effect by reference step count. If overlap vanishes within strata, it's just difficulty.

That crash was my own bookkeeping error: in run 36 I named the flipped-problem list `fl`, which overwrote a helper of the same name that `chains` depends on. Nothing was measured and no data was affected. I'll move the list to a new name, restore the original helper from its source block, and rerun the same comparison unchanged. What I'm looking for is unchanged too: a mediator that moves on E4's flipped problems but not on the E1 control.

The review refused that block and gave no reasons, so I can only guess why. The one unusual thing in it was running code extracted from an earlier block with `exec`, which means the code that ran wasn't visible in the block itself. The rest was the same text comparison on generated answers. I won't try to work around the review, but I can remove that element properly: I'll write the small number-parsing helper out as ordinary code, so everything that runs can be read directly, and record the refusal in my notes. The analysis itself uses only the text of the generated answers, no activations and no weights. If this version is refused too, I'll drop it and get the mediator evidence another way.

The question is unchanged: which mediator moves on E4's flipped problems but not on the E1 control?

The refusal has passed, and the analysis ran using only the text of the answers.

The result rules out most of what I suspected. On the 60 same-problem pairs from E4, Let was right 35% of the time and Here 13%, but false equations (0.145 vs 0.136), missing numbers (equal) and short solutions barely differ, so arithmetic and number coverage don't carry this effect. Restating does differ (problem words covered, 0.79 vs 0.64), but the E1 control shows it isn't enough: there it moved even more (0.49 to 0.71) and accuracy didn't change at all. By the test I set, no mediator I measured qualifies.

Two hints remain:
- **E1 control:** forced-Let answers do more of the work (more steps, fewer dropped numbers), yet end on a reference intermediate twice as often (0.061 to 0.136, ± 0.044 on the difference), which suggests they report the wrong quantity.
- **Question overlap:** the first-line effect survives step stratification at +9.1 ± 3.5 points. That's still only a correlation, because steps are just one part of difficulty.

Both suggest a possible goal-tracking failure, where the model computes facts but loses what was asked. The early "We want to find" statement fits this and is rare (20 of 432 Let answers), which makes it a natural branch I could test causally, the way the Let/Here flip tested the register.

First I'll measure the branch with existing data: how often "We" starts a line in Let answers, how much probability " want" gets there, and whether the goal-mention effect also survives step stratification. I'll also check whether Let's wrong finals differ from the last computed value, and pull my E1 recipe so a test edit is built consistently. If " want" has real probability at "We" and the effect survives stratification, I'll build a test. If not, I'll drop it.
